clue.text: Woman to spoil end of party

parts.note: to mar something is to spoil or damage it

indicators.note: The end of a word is its final character, so only the last letter of the word that follows is taken.

parts.note: the last letter of partY

explanation.walkthrough: A four-letter clue with two chunks and no indicator worth the name is Everyman easing you in, and the surface, a woman ruining the fun, holds together perfectly.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary is a common woman's given name, so the definition works by example rather than by meaning.

clue.text: With a prune, mint sauce or nuts will give you substantial fare

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters are scrambled into a new order
with a prune means the word mint is given a trim, losing its final letter

explanation.surface: A cook's tip: serve prunes with mint sauce or nuts for a filling dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prune' looks like a dried plum on the menu, but 'With a prune' trims MINT to MIN; MIN plus SAUCE and OR are then rearranged, as 'nuts' signals.
explanation.definitionFit: The main course is the largest and most filling dish of a meal, so it is the substantial fare.

clue.text: Entire term ghastly — not going to work any more

definitions.text: not going to work any more
definitions.note: The definition describes a person's situation while the answer is the noun naming that situation; the setter lets the state stand in for the word for it.

indicators.note: Something ghastly is in a dreadful state, and letters in a dreadful state are not left in the order they arrived in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a schoolteacher complaining about a bad term, and every word of that complaint is either raw material or the instruction to shuffle it.
explanation.definitionFit: Retirement is the state of having given up work for good, which is what no longer going in each day amounts to.

clue.text: In favour of British getting into narcotic juice: disgrace!

indicators.note: Getting into a thing means ending up inside it, so the pieces just named are planted within the word that follows.

parts.note: opium is the dried juice of the poppy, so the two words are one thing, not two
pro = in favour of, as in the pros and cons
br. is the standard shorthand for British

explanation.walkthrough: 'Narcotic juice' looks like two separate pieces of wordplay and is a single definition. Once the poppy is spotted, the drug wraps round the other three letters and the exclamation mark is pure surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Opprobrium is the public scorn and shame heaped on someone, which is what being in disgrace attracts.

clue.text: Assembled accommodation in anticipation of the Beatles

definitions.note: The answer is plural and 'accommodation' is a mass noun in British English, which covers any number of dwellings at once.

parts.note: pre- is the prefix meaning before, so anticipating something is standing in front of it
the Beatles were the Fab Four, and the Fabs for short

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman is dating himself twice over: the Fabs belong to the sixties and the houses to the years after the war, when factory-built homes went up in weeks on bombed streets.
explanation.definitionFit: Prefabs are prefabricated buildings, delivered as factory-made sections and put together on site, so they are accommodation that arrives assembled.

clue.text: Musician, somewhat gross, in isolation

indicators.note: Somewhat means only partly, and the part meant is a run of the clue's own letters rather than a whole word.

parts.note: the run starts inside the first word and carries straight on across the comma

explanation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat gross' does what a good hidden-word clue must: it reads as an aside about the musician, and the letters sit in plain sight while you look for a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Rossini wrote The Barber of Seville and William Tell, so 'musician' points at the composer by class rather than defining the name.

clue.text: Public transport lines not beginning to reach flash commercial area

parts.note: a bus is a form of public transport

indicators.note: not beginning means the word loses its first letter

parts.note: a spark is a brief flash of light

explanation.surface: Bus routes that don't start up mean nobody reaches the gleaming new shopping district.
explanation.walkthrough: BUS, then INES (lines without its first letter), then SPARK for 'flash'.
explanation.definitionFit: A business park is an area of offices and commercial buildings, often on the edge of a town.

clue.text: About time: Everyman twice sent up as 'particular'

indicators.note: in a down clue, sent up means the letters are read upwards, so backwards
about means the setter's letters go around the time letter

parts.note: the setter Everyman refers to himself twice, once as ME and once as I

explanation.surface: The setter, after a while, gets himself teased twice for being fussy.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is ME and I; around T that makes METI, and 'sent up' turns it upside down in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A particular is an individual detail or point, and an item is likewise a single detail in a list.

clue.text: Primarily: marry / amigo / tisane / ending!

indicators.note: What comes primarily comes first, so only the opening character of each word in the list is wanted.

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the four listed words, read in order

explanation.walkthrough: Every word in the list also means the answer: to marry is to mate, mate is chess for the ending, and mate is a South American tisane. The setter has clued it four times and spelled it once.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is Spanish for friend, and in British English your mate is exactly that, a friend or companion.

clue.text: Letter from Athens returned to you in Paris

indicators.note: Something returned comes back the way it came, so the phrase is read from its final letter to its first.

parts.note: in French, 'to you' is a toi, and naming a French city is the standard way of asking for French

explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter from Athens returned' reads as post going back unopened, and both halves are doing something else: Athens means the Greek alphabet and the letters travel backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Iota is the ninth letter of the Greek alphabet, so 'from Athens' points at the alphabet rather than at correspondence.

clue.text: According to sibling, canvas is fixed

parts.note: per = according to, as in 'per your email'
sis is the familiar short form of sister
canvas is what one is made of, and 'under canvas' means camping

explanation.walkthrough: Three ordinary words in a row with nothing marking the joins, which is what makes a long charade hard: the surface is a remark about an artist's stretched canvas and never stumbles.
explanation.definitionFit: Something persistent keeps on without shifting, which is 'fixed' in the sense of steadfast and unbudging rather than mended.

clue.text: Doubt value of pre-euro currency?

parts.note: to question something is to doubt it
Germany spent the mark until the euro arrived in 2002

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the last character of the clue rather than a word in it: the setter writes the thing itself and leaves you to notice. Read without it, the sentence is nothing but wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue ends with the punctuation it defines, the sign written to show that something is being asked or cast into doubt.

clue.text: Number of readers an issue for first-aider

definitions.meaning: a newspaper's reach is measured by how many copies get out to buyers
first aid is taught as airway, breathing and then keeping the blood moving

explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' is placed to keep you in the newsroom, where it means an edition; for the first-aider it means a problem, and the two trades share one word without a join between them.
explanation.definitionFit: One word covers a paper's readership figure and the flow of blood round a body, which is what a first-aider checks for.

clue.text: Empty bath containing ooze onto river: that's novel

indicators.note: onto means in this down clue the first part sits on top of the river
containing means the outer letters hold the word for ooze between them
empty means take away the inside, leaving just the outer letters

parts.note: the word bath, emptied to its first and last letters B and H
to leak is to ooze out slowly
the Ouse is a river in Yorkshire and another in East Anglia

explanation.surface: An empty bath has sludge seeping into a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Empty' leaves B and H of bath, 'containing' puts LEAK between them, and 'onto' sets that on top of OUSE, an English river.
explanation.definitionFit: Bleak House is a novel by Charles Dickens, published in instalments from 1852 to 1853.

clue.text: Cricketers arranged friendlies

indicators.note: Fixtures get arranged and so do letters, and letters arranged afresh come out in a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, one of them the definition and one the instruction, so the fodder has to be the remaining one. 'Arranged friendlies' is such natural sports-desk English that neither job shows.
explanation.definitionFit: Fielders posted close to the bat inside the ring make up the in-field, so 'cricketers' defines them by their position.

clue.text: Kim disheartened; Susan sadly shows up

indicators.note: Sadly marks something that has gone wrong, and letters gone wrong are letters out of their proper order.
To be disheartened is to lose heart, and a word's heart is the letter sitting at its centre.

parts.note: the name loses its central letter and keeps the two either side
anagram fodder, five letters

explanation.walkthrough: Two ordinary first names are the hardest fodder to spot, because nothing about Kim or Susan looks like raw material until you count the letters against the enumeration.
explanation.definitionFit: To unmask someone is to show them up for what they really are, using 'show up' in its exposing sense rather than its arriving one.

clue.text: Regulator cutting short abuse: cool

indicators.note: cutting short means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: abuse, as a noun, is insult
in means fashionable, cool

explanation.surface: A referee curtails the abuse and keeps everyone calm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regulator' suggests a person keeping order, but it is the hormone; IN is the fashionable sense of cool.
explanation.definitionFit: Insulin is the hormone that regulates the level of glucose in the blood.

clue.text: Take time here on cloudless day

definitions.meaning: the surface invites you to be unhurried; the setter means take a reading of the hour off the object itself
it tells you nothing at all under an overcast sky, which points at what powers it

explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to hunt for here, only one sly sentence. 'Cloudless day' is more than scenery: the instrument is named for the very thing it needs to work at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A shadow thrown by a gnomon creeps round a marked plate as the earth turns, so the hour can be read off it in sunshine.

clue.text: Eagerly approached meadow with dung covering rabbit's tail

parts.note: a lea is a poetic word for a meadow

indicators.note: covering means the dung goes over the tail letter, holding it inside

parts.note: a pat is a flat lump of dung, as in cowpat

indicators.note: tail means the last letter of the rabbit

parts.note: the possessive just says the tail belongs to the word rabbit, whose last letter is T

explanation.surface: In a field, a pile of dung lands on a rabbit's bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: LEA, then PAT 'covering' the T that is the rabbit's 'tail', its last letter; P, T and AT give PTAT.
explanation.definitionFit: To leap at a chance is to seize it eagerly, so the past tense means eagerly approached.

clue.text: Singers giving appeasing gift to Indian princess

parts.note: a sop is something handed over to placate someone, as in a sop to Cerberus
a rani is an Indian queen or princess, the feminine of raja

explanation.walkthrough: The English plural would end in -OS, and the crossing letter shows the setter has gone to the opera house for the Italian one instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Soprani is the Italian plural of soprano, the highest voices in a choir, so it names singers by their range.

clue.text: Furtively approach drink, hiding empty

indicators.note: A thing hidden is put out of sight inside something else, so this piece is buried in the letters beside it.

parts.note: to sup is to drink, and supper takes its name from it
an idle boast or an idle threat is an empty one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink, hiding empty' is a whole little scene of someone concealing a drained glass, and both nouns in it are synonyms doing wordplay instead.
explanation.definitionFit: To sidle up to someone is to edge towards them sideways and unnoticed, which is a furtive approach in one movement.

clue.text: Palaeolithic man tilled earthen land

indicators.note: Tilled ground has been turned over and broken up, and letters given that treatment come out in a different order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.walkthrough: The picture of a man working his fields is tens of thousands of years too late for the answer, whose people hunted and gathered and tilled nothing at all. That gap is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Neanderthals were the archaic humans of the Palaeolithic, so the definition names them by their era.

clue.text: So it's hours being regularly wasted

indicators.note: Wasting at regular intervals throws away every other character, and what survives is read straight through.

parts.note: take the second letter and then every second one after it, counting the s of the contraction as a letter like any other

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe earns its keep: the count runs through it as though it were not there, which is what stops the fodder looking like fodder in so short a clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Thus and so both mean 'in this way', the adverb pointing back at whatever has just been said.

clue.text: Antagonistic to some characters from Pleasant Island

indicators.note: Characters are letters as well as people, and taking some of them means lifting a run out of what follows.

parts.note: the old European name for Nauru, in the Pacific, carries the letters wanted straight across the gap between its two words

explanation.walkthrough: A capital letter mid-clue usually means a proper noun, and this one is a colonial name for a Pacific island - pleasant enough on the surface to hide something hostile.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is anti is set against whatever is under discussion, which is the hostile stance the definition names.

clue.text: Spooner's to corral lusty types for women's gatherings

indicators.note: Spooner's means the opening sounds of the two words are swapped, as Reverend Spooner did

parts.note: to pen animals is to corral them
hearties are hearty, vigorous people, said here as HARTIES

explanation.surface: Reverend Spooner's own words for rounding up boisterous people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen hearties' with the starting sounds swapped is heard as the answer. The Reverend William Spooner was famous for slips like this.
explanation.definitionFit: Hen parties are celebrations held by women, usually for a bride-to-be before her wedding.

clue.text: Cut into pieces: eight or 27, perhaps

definitions.meaning: in the kitchen you chop meat or vegetables into small even blocks
two multiplied by itself three times, and three treated the same way

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut into pieces' looks exactly like an anagram instruction, which is the trap; it is a plain definition, and the second one arrives as arithmetic. The question mark admits the numbers are only examples.
explanation.definitionFit: To cube food is to cut it into small blocks, and a cube number is what you get multiplying a number by itself three times.

clue.text: Aggro given by ultimately snarky, flippant imitator: this'll help you hold things together

definitions.text: this'll help you hold things together

parts.note: aggro is British slang for trouble, and to give someone stick is to give them a hard time

indicators.note: Ultimately points at the end of a thing, so the final letter is taken - here from each of the two adjectives it governs.

parts.note: the closing letters of the two adjectives, in the order they are written
to ape someone is to imitate them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' governs both adjectives at once, and that is where solvers stall: take one last letter and the count comes up short by one.
explanation.definitionFit: Sticky tape is the everyday clear adhesive roll used on paper and parcels, which the definition describes rather than names.

clue.text: Overheard one inspiring announcements from Persians

indicators.note: Something overheard is caught by ear alone, so the spelling wanted is the other one that sounds the same.

parts.note: one of the nine Muses is what inspires a poet, and said aloud she is spelled quite differently

explanation.walkthrough: The capital P wants you to think of people from Persia. The Persians here are cats, and what they are announcing is dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: A Persian is a long-haired breed of cat, and the noise a cat makes to announce itself is a mew.
